stories.headline: US says it disabled three Iranian oil tankers after attack
stories.dek: The Pentagon said US warships came under missile fire near key oil routes, and two Iranian tankers were left disabled.
paragraphs: The US military said Saturday it struck three Iranian oil tankers after Iranian missiles targeted a US aircraft carrier and a destroyer in regional waters. It said no US personnel were hurt. The strikes mark a fresh escalation after a week of renewed fighting and failed diplomacy.

This war began on February 28 with US and Israeli attacks on Iran, then moved in bursts between combat and talks. Iran and the US have since hit military and economic targets. The tankers were struck near Kharg Island, near Jask, and in the Gulf of Oman.

It is still unclear how Iran will respond, whether shipping through the Strait of Hormuz will face new disruption, and whether oil exports will fall further. Nuclear talks have collapsed. Civilian risk is also unresolved after recent US strikes in southern Iran killed at least five people.
stories.changes: For ordinary readers, this raises the risk of higher energy prices and more disruption to shipping through a route used for global oil and gas trade.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean a full regional war is certain today, and the US said its ships and crews were not hit.

cover.title: US disables three Iranian oil tankers after missile attack at sea
cover.standfirst: The US military said it struck three Iranian oil tankers on Saturday after missiles targeted a US aircraft carrier and destroyer in regional waters. Two tankers were left disabled and one was destroyed. The action adds to a renewed week of fighting near the Strait of Hormuz.

art.label: Silkscreen
art.concept: A hard black aerial silhouette of the Strait of Hormuz fills the upper two-thirds of the cover, the coasts closing into a narrow choke point. Through that black, carve a white channel whose shape resolves on second look into a disabled oil tanker split into two drifting sections, one half slewing off course; a single red missile trail cuts across the strait toward the break, slightly off-register so it trembles with alarm. Keep the lower third as near-empty dark sea, with only the faintest wake remnants, so type can sit cleanly.
art.note: Grim and spare; black sea, rust red fire, ash grey smoke.
art.second_beat: First you see the chokepoint under attack; then you realize the water gap is also the broken tanker, making the route itself the casualty.

stories.headline: Putin orders three-day halt to strikes on Kyiv during US visit
stories.dek: The Kremlin said the pause starts at midnight as Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner travel to Moscow and then Kyiv.
paragraphs: Russia says it will stop strikes on Kyiv for 72 hours from midnight, while U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visit Moscow and prepare to travel on to Kyiv. The Kremlin linked the pause directly to the visit. Ukraine has said it will also suspend airstrikes during the envoys' time in the country.

The trip comes after weeks of heavier air attacks by both sides, more than four years after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Russia has stepped up drone and missile strikes on Kyiv and other cities, while Ukraine has used long-range drones and missiles against targets inside Russia. Fighting on the front line has changed little.

It is not clear whether the pause will hold, whether it applies only to Kyiv, or whether it could lead to wider talks. Kremlin officials said there were no new peace ideas on the table. Russian strikes outside Kyiv continued to kill and injure civilians, and Ukraine has warned it may adjust its own operations after the visit.
stories.changes: For people in Kyiv, the next three days may bring a brief drop in air attacks while the U.S. delegation is in town.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean a ceasefire, a peace deal, or an end to Russian attacks elsewhere in Ukraine.

cover.title: Russia halts strikes on Kyiv for three days during US visit
cover.standfirst: The Kremlin said Vladimir Putin ordered a 72-hour pause in strikes on Kyiv from midnight as U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visit Moscow and then Ukraine. Kyiv said it would also halt airstrikes during the visit, but fighting and attacks elsewhere have not stopped.

art.label: Silkscreen
art.concept: A night view of Kyiv in near-black silhouette, kept low so the lower third stays mostly empty for type. Across the upper half, a passenger jet passes overhead as a hard black underside, wings spanning the page; from the city below, a single red anti-aircraft searchlight rises toward it but stops dead halfway up, cut off cleanly so the aircraft crosses through a dark gap of withheld fire. Keep everything reduced to three elements only: skyline, jet, truncated beam.
art.note: Tense and restrained, with deep black, cold blue, and one muted red accent.
art.second_beat: First you see a plane over a war city; a beat later you realise the danger has not gone away, it has merely been forcibly stopped mid-action for a fixed pause.

stories.headline: US envoys arrive in Moscow for new Ukraine peace push
stories.dek: Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner landed in Moscow as Russia announced a 72-hour pause in airstrikes on Kyiv.
paragraphs: US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Moscow on September 5 to restart talks on ending Russia’s war in Ukraine. President Donald Trump said they carried a formal peace proposal. Russia also announced a 72-hour halt to airstrikes on Kyiv during the visit, giving the talks immediate weight.

Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, and the war is now in its fifth year. Earlier US-led talks in late 2025 and January 2026 did not produce a deal. The new proposal is reported to include input from European allies and Ukrainian officials, and the envoys are due to travel on to Kyiv next.

Nothing important is settled yet. The hardest issues remain the same: occupied territory, Ukraine’s future security guarantees, and Russia’s demands over NATO. It is also unclear whether Vladimir Putin will meet the US envoys, whether Kyiv accepts the plan, or whether the temporary pause in strikes will hold.
stories.changes: This creates a new opening for talks and may briefly reduce attacks on Kyiv while diplomats meet.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean the war is close to ending, and no ceasefire or settlement has been agreed.

cover.title: US envoys arrive in Moscow as Russia pauses strikes on Kyiv
cover.standfirst: Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner landed in Moscow on September 5 with a Trump administration peace proposal for the war in Ukraine. Russia then announced a 72-hour halt to airstrikes on Kyiv, and the envoys are expected to continue on to Kyiv after meetings in Moscow.

art.label: Maximalist doodle
art.concept: A single descending airliner on final approach over Moscow is replaced entirely by a rolled peace proposal: the fuselage is a curled sheaf of paper, with two stiff folded pages reading as wings and tail, so it unmistakably flies first and only then reveals itself as fragile paperwork. Below, render Moscow in dense maximalist doodle with Saint Basil’s domes, ring-road loops, embassy sedans, radar dishes and air-defence launchers, but keep the lower third largely open as a pale runway-like strip with only a few tiny ground vehicles, so type can sit cleanly across it.
art.note: Tense and procedural; muted red, black, slate gray.
art.second_beat: First you see a plane arriving in Moscow; a beat later you realise the aircraft is only paperwork, making the peace push feel exposed as it enters an armed capital.

stories.headline: US takes stake in company tied to Venezuelan oilfields
stories.dek: A new deal gives the Pentagon equity, supply rights and board influence over a private company with access to 17 Venezuelan oilfields.
paragraphs: The Trump administration has backed a deal that gives the Pentagon a 35% stake in North American Blue Energy Partners, a private company with century-long concessions to 17 Venezuelan oilfields. The White House says the arrangement secures oil for national needs and reduces Chinese and Russian influence in Venezuela.

The deal follows last year's US-backed removal of Nicolás Maduro and the installation of an interim government led by Delcy Rodríguez. Venezuela then granted the Barbados-based company access to fields holding 65 billion barrels of proven reserves, according to the White House, a volume that would rank among the world's largest.

It is still unclear whether the reserves and production targets will prove real, whether private investors will follow, and how legal and political risks will be handled. Critics say the structure gives the US de facto control of a foreign oil company and ties Washington to a businessman with a disputed record.
stories.changes: It gives the US government direct leverage over part of Venezuela's future oil output and could shape fuel security and foreign policy for years.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean the US suddenly owns all Venezuelan oil or that gasoline prices will quickly change for drivers.

cover.title: US takes stake in company controlling Venezuelan oilfields
cover.standfirst: The Trump administration approved a deal that gives the Pentagon a 35% stake in a private oil company with rights to 17 Venezuelan fields. The US also gets priority access to output at production cost, while officials say the arrangement is meant to secure supply and limit Chinese and Russian influence.

art.label: Punk cutout
art.concept: On a flat signal-red ground, run a tight diagonal stream of identical blunt black oil barrels from upper left toward lower right, as if they are being unloaded or rolling into supply. Near the centre, one barrel alone is open: its lid flips back and a stark white Pentagon silhouette is caught mid-drop into the opening, perfectly aligned so it reads as being posted straight into the oil itself. Keep the lower third mostly clear red, with only a few cropped barrel rims intruding at the top edge of that space.
art.note: Sharp, critical, high-contrast; black, dirty gold, deep red.
art.second_beat: First you see a flow of oil barrels; then the single opened one makes the whole reserve read as oil becoming a Pentagon-held asset.

stories.headline: Global food prices reach highest level since 2022
stories.dek: Black Sea shipping problems linked to the Russia-Ukraine war have driven wheat futures about 30% higher than a year ago.
paragraphs: Global food prices have climbed to their highest level since 2022, with wheat a main driver. The immediate pressure comes from disrupted exports through the Black Sea, where the Russia-Ukraine war has made shipping less reliable and more costly. That has pushed wheat futures sharply higher.

Ukraine and Russia are both major grain exporters, and Black Sea ports are a key route for wheat sold to buyers in Africa, the Middle East and Asia. When shipments slow or insurance and transport costs rise, importers pay more. Those higher costs can then feed into bread, flour and other staples.

It is still unclear how long the disruption will last or whether other exporters can fill the gap fast enough. Prices can also swing with harvest forecasts, weather and government trade limits. For now, the main unresolved issue is whether Black Sea exports can move steadily again.
stories.changes: Food-importing countries and shoppers may face higher prices for bread, flour and other wheat-based basics if the rise lasts.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean immediate shortages everywhere, and it does not mean every grocery price will jump at once.

cover.title: Global food prices rise as Black Sea wheat exports falter
cover.standfirst: Global food prices have reached their highest point since 2022 after Black Sea disruption linked to the Russia-Ukraine war hit wheat exports. Wheat futures are about 30% above a year ago, adding pressure to importers and raising the risk of higher prices for bread and other staples.

art.label: Drawn chart
art.concept: Draw a bare bar chart rising left to right across the upper two-thirds, with a quiet empty lower third for type. The final and tallest bar is replaced by a simplified cargo ship standing upright like a bar, its bow tipped slightly as a few grain kernels spill from the deck; keep all earlier bars plain, and put only this ship-bar and the very top edge in the accent colour so the shipping disruption unmistakably becomes the peak in food prices.
art.note: Clear, sober, muted tan and navy palette.
art.second_beat: At first it reads as a price chart; a beat later you see the tallest bar is a destabilised grain ship, so the cause of the spike has literally taken over the statistic.

stories.headline: US regulators review Tesla Cybercab safety certification after Austin launch
stories.dek: The audit began one day after Tesla put two-seat taxis without steering wheels or pedals onto Austin streets.
paragraphs: US auto safety regulators opened an investigation into Tesla’s new Cybercabs one day after the company launched the service in Austin. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration is checking whether Tesla properly certified the vehicles under federal rules, because the taxis lack steering wheels, mirrors and brake pedals.

Tesla says it used the normal self-certification process that carmakers use before putting new vehicles on public roads. But regulators do not audit every filing. They step in when they think a certification may break federal standards. The Cybercab is unusual because passengers have no manual controls in an emergency.

The audit will examine Tesla’s certification process and technical data, but regulators have not yet said whether the Cybercabs must stop operating. Tesla also faces other federal safety probes into its self-driving systems, including crashes in low visibility, red-light incidents and delayed crash reporting.
stories.changes: If you planned to use Tesla’s new robotaxi service, expect closer scrutiny and possible changes to how quickly it expands.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean all Tesla robotaxis are banned or that the Austin service must shut down today.

cover.title: US regulators investigate Tesla Cybercabs after Austin launch
cover.standfirst: Federal auto safety regulators began an audit a day after Tesla launched its new two-seat Cybercabs in Austin. The vehicles have no steering wheel, mirrors or brake pedal. Officials will review Tesla’s self-certification records and technical data before deciding whether the taxis fully meet federal safety rules.

art.label: Object photograph
art.concept: On a clean off-white seamless, stage two ruled, official-looking vehicle forms side by side with a quiet lower third left open for type. On the left, a generic yellow die-cast taxi sits fully centered and compliant on its sheet; on the right, a unmistakably Cybercab-like silver two-seat model with a smooth nose and dark glass has rolled forward so far that half the car hangs off the document’s edge into empty space, front wheels suspended, as if it has left certification before the paper could hold it. Keep everything else out: no extra props, no text, just the tension of the car tipping from paperwork into the street.
art.note: Cool, procedural mood; muted reds, asphalt gray, cream and black.
art.second_beat: First read: two vehicles on two forms; second beat: the Tesla has already moved beyond certification, making the launch-before-settlement the story.

stories.headline: Greek F-4 jet crashes during air show near Athens
stories.dek: The pilots' fate was not immediately known after the military aircraft went down during a public display near the Greek capital.
paragraphs: A Greek F-4 military jet crashed during an air show near Athens, according to early reports filed two hours ago. The accident happened during a public event, which is why the condition of people on the ground matters as much as the crew in the aircraft.

The F-4 is an older fighter aircraft that has served in several air forces for decades. Air shows bring military planes close to crowds for display flying, so even a single crash quickly becomes both a rescue operation and a safety incident for spectators nearby.

Officials have not yet said what caused the crash. The fate of the pilots was not immediately known, and it remains unclear whether anyone in the crowd was injured. Investigators and emergency crews are expected to secure the site, identify the crew, and confirm any casualties.
stories.changes: If you are near the event area, expect emergency closures, delays, and tighter security until officials finish rescue work and begin an investigation.
stories.unchanged: This does not by itself show a wider attack or a broad change in Greece's air safety picture.

cover.title: Greek F-4 jet crashes during air show near Athens
cover.standfirst: A Greek military F-4 aircraft crashed during an air show near Athens on Sunday, according to early reports. The fate of the pilots was not immediately known, and officials had not yet said whether anyone in the crowd was hurt. Emergency crews are expected to secure the site and begin an investigation.

art.label: Gouache painting
art.concept: Paint one wide gouache view of the Athens air-show shoreline in bright noon light, with no hard split but a clear left-to-right turn in time: at left, a Greek F-4 Phantom banks low over blue water during the display while spectators and parasols sit as tiny calm marks along the beach; at right, the same coast has emptied into panic, with a dirty ochre-and-charcoal smoke plume rising just beyond the shore and people running inland as small dark strokes. Keep the lower third mostly open sea and pale beach for type, and place one abandoned folding chair near the centre of the transition, still facing upward toward the sky.
art.note: Sober, tense mood; muted blue-grey sky, dusty ground, black smoke.
art.second_beat: First you read the single landscape turning from air-show leisure into disaster; a beat later you notice the lone chair left behind at the hinge between the two moments.

stories.headline: Philippines vice president posts bail after arrest order
stories.dek: Sara Duterte paid 360,000 pesos in bail on three grave threat charges tied to remarks about President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
paragraphs: Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte posted bail on Saturday after a court issued an arrest order a day earlier. She faces three counts of grave threats over remarks prosecutors say targeted President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., his wife and a senior lawmaker. She denies making a real threat.

The case grows out of a 2024 online news conference, when Duterte said an assassin should kill Marcos, his wife and then-House Speaker Martin Romualdez if she herself were killed. She later said she was speaking about her own safety. The dispute sits inside a larger break between two powerful political families.

Duterte remains free while the criminal case moves ahead, and a conviction could bar her from future office, including a 2028 presidential run. Her separate Senate impeachment trial is already underway. It is still unclear how quickly either case will move or how much public support each side can hold.
stories.changes: This raises the legal and political risk around the Philippines vice president and could affect the next presidential race.
stories.unchanged: It does not remove Duterte from office now, and it does not settle the criminal case or the impeachment trial.

cover.title: Philippines vice president posts bail after arrest order
cover.standfirst: Sara Duterte appeared at a court in Metro Manila on Saturday and posted 360,000 pesos bail on three grave threat charges. Prosecutors link the case to 2024 remarks about President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., his wife and Martin Romualdez. She denies wrongdoing, and both the criminal case and her impeachment trial will continue.

art.label: Made object
art.concept: Build a handmade jail cell from thick grey pipe-cleaner bars against a plain bright backdrop, but leave one vertical bar missing and show a fat stack of unmistakably Philippine money — yellow, blue and red notes with a few peso coins pressed into the clay — being slid into that gap as the replacement bar. Stage it mid-action, slightly off-centre, with the cash-bar not quite seated so the opening still reads as a possible way through; keep the lower third clean and empty for type.
art.note: Tense and public; red, black and off-white palette.
art.second_beat: First you see a cell; then you realise money is literally doing the job of the bars, so bail reads as both confinement and release at once.

stories.headline: Tadej Pogacar ends season after Vuelta crash and neck fracture
stories.dek: The world champion will miss races in Montreal, Ljubljana and Lombardy after surgery for a broken collarbone and treatment for concussion.
paragraphs: Tadej Pogacar will not race again this season after injuries from his crash on stage eight of the Vuelta a Espana. His team said he needs more time to recover from a broken collarbone, concussion, a stable neck fracture and abrasions. The decision rules him out of this month's World Championships.

Pogacar, 27, is one of cycling's biggest riders and has won the Tour de France five times. He crashed out of the Vuelta while leading the race and chasing the only Grand Tour title missing from his record. He was also due to defend titles later this season in Europe and at Il Lombardia.

It is not yet clear when Pogacar will race again, beyond his team saying he will not return this season and will recover without a fixed deadline. The team also said he has signed a two-year contract extension through 2032. His absence leaves the World Championships without its defending men's road race champion.
stories.changes: Fans will not see Pogacar race again this year, including at the World Championships and other major autumn events.
stories.unchanged: This does not end his career, and his team says the break is to let him recover fully rather than rush back.

cover.title: Tadej Pogacar will miss rest of season after Vuelta crash
cover.standfirst: Cycling champion Tadej Pogacar will not race again this year after crashing out of the Vuelta a Espana while leading the race. His team said he suffered a broken collarbone, concussion and a stable neck fracture, so he will miss the World Championships in Montreal and other autumn races.

art.label: Decorative flat
art.concept: A single pale road runs diagonally upward through dry, decorative Spanish hills. In the upper half it is unmistakably the Vuelta at full tilt — a red race caravan, a few motorbikes, barriers, and a tight ribbon of riders — then, at a clear break in tempo, the same road continues into a quiet lower third where the race has abruptly ended: no peloton, just an ambulance receding, a few barriers being folded away, and one tiny rainbow-striped rider-shape disappearing with the medical convoy. Keep the lower third broad and calm for type; use only the minimum vehicles, barriers and riders needed to make the before/after legible at a glance.
art.note: Somber but clean; muted road greys with the rainbow bands as the only bright color.
art.second_beat: First you see a race route split into full and empty; second you realise the same road has turned from competition into withdrawal, with the world champion carried out of the season.

stories.headline: Justice Department expands scrutiny of Fauci and other virus scientists
stories.dek: A federal inquiry appears to reach beyond Anthony Fauci to a broader group of researchers tied to pandemic-era science.
paragraphs: The Justice Department is pursuing an investigation that includes Anthony Fauci and other virus scientists, according to the report. The effort appears broader than the public fights in Congress and has drawn new attention because it reaches a wider circle of researchers involved in pandemic-era work.

Fauci became a central political target during and after the Covid pandemic, especially among congressional Republicans. Public criticism focused on his advice, his role in the federal response, and questions about virus research. This report says federal investigators have been examining more people than the public debate around Fauci alone suggested.

It is still unclear what conduct investigators are examining, how many scientists are involved, or whether any charges will result. The report summary does not say what stage the inquiry has reached. It also leaves open how the investigation could affect research institutions, public trust, and future work on dangerous pathogens.
stories.changes: Readers may see more legal and political scrutiny of pandemic researchers, not just Anthony Fauci.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean any scientist has been charged or that established public health findings have been overturned.

cover.title: Justice Department investigates Fauci and other virus scientists
cover.standfirst: A reported federal inquiry goes beyond Anthony Fauci to a wider group of researchers linked to pandemic-era virus science. The scope, legal theory, and number of people involved remain unclear, and there is no public sign yet of charges or a final decision.

art.label: Punk cutout
art.concept: On a flat signal-red ground, a coarse black fishing net is being cast in from the upper left, caught mid-spread as it drops over a small scatter of stark white-and-gray photocopy-cutout lab objects: a Petri dish, a micropipette, a specimen vial rack, and a few loose sample tubes. One central tube is singled out with a brutal black marker circle, but the net clearly engulfs everything around it; keep the lower third largely open, with the objects clustered just above it, and strip away any extra marks or background detail.
art.note: Cold, suspicious mood; muted beige, gray, navy, and surgical blue.
art.second_beat: First you see a raid-like net dropping; a beat later you get that the inquiry has widened from one circled figure to an entire field of pandemic-era science.
